## Description

Adaptive Simpson quadrature approximates $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ to a requested tolerance $\varepsilon$ by recursively halving intervals until a local error estimate passes, so small subintervals appear only where $f$ needs them.
On an interval $[a,b]$ with midpoint $m$,
$$
S(a,b)=\frac{b-a}{6}\left[f(a)+4f(m)+f(b)\right],
$$
and refinement compares $S(a,b)$ against $S(a,m)+S(m,b)$, which needs only two new values of $f$, at the quarter-points.

The animation uses the acceptance test of Mathews' routine: $[a,b]$ is accepted when
$$
\left|S(a,m)+S(m,b)-S(a,b)\right| < \varepsilon_{[a,b]},
$$
where the whole interval starts with $\varepsilon$ and each half of a split interval gets half its tolerance, so refinement concentrates where curvature or oscillation is strongest.
An accepted interval contributes $S(a,m)+S(m,b)$ to the result.
A common variant uses $15\,\varepsilon_{[a,b]}$ on the right; for the example below it accepts 9 subintervals (the finest is $[0,1/32]$) instead of 20 (the finest is $[0,1/2048]$).

The test rests on a general result that needs $f\in C^4$ on each interval.
Simpson's error on an interval of width $w$ is $-\tfrac{w^5}{2880}f^{(4)}(c)$ for some $c$ in it, so halving the interval divides the error by about 16, and if $f^{(4)}$ is nearly constant across $[a,b]$,
$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-\bigl[S(a,m)+S(m,b)\bigr]\approx\frac{S(a,m)+S(m,b)-S(a,b)}{15}.
$$
Under that assumption each accepted interval's error is below about $\varepsilon_{[a,b]}/15$, and because each split divides a tolerance between two halves, the accepted tolerances add up to exactly $\varepsilon$; the total error is then at most about $\varepsilon/15$, an estimate rather than a guaranteed bound.
In [Case 1](#case-1) the routine's value $2.016273$ is within $7.1\times10^{-6}$ of the integral, well inside $\varepsilon=10^{-3}$, even though $f$ is not $C^4$ at $x=0$.
There the error on $[0,w]$ shrinks only like $w^{5/3}$, and on $[0,1/2048]$ it is about 7 times the estimate, yet under its tolerance.

The test sees only five values of $f$ per interval and can be fooled.
For $f(x)=\sin^2(4\pi x)$ on $[0,1]$, all five samples are $0$, so the first test passes (at $\varepsilon=10^{-3}$ or $10^{-6}$) and the routine returns $0$ for an integral of $1/2$.
Mathews' routine also has no limit on the depth of recursion.
For the step $f(x)=0$ on $[0,1/3)$ and $1$ on $[1/3,1]$, the interval holding the jump fails the test at every level, since $|S(a,m)+S(m,b)-S(a,b)|$ and the tolerance both shrink in proportion to its width; the recursion stops at depth 54 only when a floating-point midpoint rounds onto an endpoint.

[Simpson's Rule](../simpsons-rule-for-numerical-integration/) applies the same formula with one fixed step size; adding the error estimate to $S(a,m)+S(m,b)$ is one [Richardson Extrapolation](../richardson-extrapolation/) step and gives [Boole's Rule](../booles-rule/) on the interval, as in [Romberg Integration](../romberg-integration/).

## Animations

Each animation below shows the **adaptive Simpson refinement process** for
$f(x)=1+e^{-x}\sin(8x^{2/3})$ on $[0,2]$ with tolerance $\varepsilon=10^{-3}$. Starting from the single panel $[0,2]$, each frame splits the widest panel that fails the test (leftmost first, except that $[1/2,1]$ is split before $[0,1/2]$, as in Mathews' trace) and marks the two new sample points in blue; "Approximation" is the composite Simpson sum of $S(a,b)$ over the panels drawn.

Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

### Case 1 — Adaptive Refinement, $f(x)=1+e^{-x}\sin(8x^{2/3})$, $[0,2]$, $\varepsilon=10^{-3}$ {#case-1}

**Behavior:** Refinement stops when all 20 panels pass the test. The 41 points drawn are the nodes of the composite rule; the test also evaluates each panel's two quarter-points, so reaching this partition samples $f$ at 81 distinct points. $[1.5,2]$ is never split, while 19 of the 41 nodes lie in $[0,1/8]$. The last seven frames split $[0,1/16], [0,1/32], \dots, [0,1/1024]$ in turn, because $f'$ is unbounded at $x=0$ ($f'(x)\approx \tfrac{16}{3}x^{-1/3}$ near $0$); the panels split in the last five frames are at most $1/64$ wide (under 5 pixels at this scale), so the blue label names each one. The final estimate $2.016252$ differs from the integral $2.016280$ by $-2.8\times10^{-5}$; summing $S(a,m)+S(m,b)$ over the same panels, as the recursive routine returns, gives $2.016273$.
